BERT4Rec’s random masked-item reconstruction differs from appended-MASK next-item prediction: reconstruction can exploit right context unavailable at inference. [Recency Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643) explicitly identifies this weak correspondence and associated training inefficiency. Recent related work includes [Sequential Masked Modeling (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11150) and [Masked History Learning (2025; revised 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23649), which combines historical reconstruction with next-item learning in a generative recommender. These motivate testing objective transfer, but do not establish that reconstruction helps this particular BERT4Rec checkpoint.

The closest diagnostic precedent is [Task Affinity Grouping](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=hqDb8d65Vfh): apply a hypothetical update from objective A, then measure objective B’s relative loss reduction, Z = 1 − L_B(after)/L_B(before). Positive values indicate local benefit; negative values indicate harm. [Gradient Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.05847) likewise defines transfer through loss reduction. Gradient cosine alone omits update magnitude, optimizer preconditioning and finite-step curvature; an actual virtual update measures their combined local effect.

Proposed adaptation: on the same checkpoint, update using reconstruction targets from public training prefixes, then evaluate terminal cross-entropy and positive-versus-negative ranking margins on disjoint prefixes. Compare reconstruction, terminal-only and no-update controls; match target counts and report update norms. Probe embeddings and Transformer blocks separately across a small step-size grid. Use fixed candidates and controlled dropout; restore parameters, buffers, optimizer and RNG state after every probe. This is a diagnostic proposal, not an established BERT4Rec result: short-step benefit need not predict eventual HR@10. It requires no independently fitted predictor or score fusion.
